title: HAQQ Legal Agent Study: A Long-Horizon Legal AI Benchmark [LOW-RELIABILITY — DERIVATIVE OF HARVEY LAB, DO NOT CITE FOR ITS RESULTS]
author: Stephane Boghossian

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s distinction between narrow question-answering and dependable completion of legal assignments, and materially develops it through partner-style instructions, document-heavy matter files, reviewable work products and all-pass grading. Its reported comparative results are unverified because the source is expressly low-reliability and derivative, so they do not establish actual system performance.
qs: There is no partial credit on the partner's review.'  How do frontier AI models score on long-horizon legal work?

Study tasks mirror how work actually arrives: a ~50-word partner-style instruction plus a matter folder mixing material documents with noise, requiring a reviewable work product (memo, redline, draft pleading) graded by expert rubric.

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: HAQQ accepts the cluster’s core case for realistic, task-specific evaluation and strict completion metrics, then materially extends it toward multilingual, civil-law and MENA matters and explicit distinctions between autonomous completion and lawyer-assisted use. Its vendor-built, derivative and partly prospective methodology limits its value as independent performance evidence.
qs: A long-horizon evaluation measuring whether AI agents can do real legal work end-to-end, not just answer trivia: 1,372 tasks across 24 practice areas graded against ~78,000 atomic, binary pass/fail rubric criteria, with civil-law and MENA coverage by design.
Aggregate scores hide the operational question every law firm partner asks: which kinds of work can I delegate end-to-end, which need a lawyer in the loop, and which I shouldn't touch?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s call for task- and use-context-specific evaluation by proposing a jurisdictionally broader benchmark built from realistic, associate-level matters that require contextual relevance judgment and cross-document synthesis. It provides benchmark design rather than performance evidence, so it does not establish capability, productivity or autonomy claims.
qs: We started from real matters - anonymized, sanitized - handled by practicing lawyers across our customer base.
The agent must determine which files matter, read them in context, and synthesize the relevant provisions across the matter.

It also uses expert-written atomic criteria for diagnosis and training, but supplies design rationales rather than comparative validation of reliability or professional-quality measurement.

kp.k: Corpus flags this vendor account as low reliability
kp.d: The supplied document labels this 2026 HAQQ company-blog account by Stephane Boghossian as low-reliability, derivative of Harvey LAB, and not to be cited for its results. The points below therefore describe the article's arguments and proposed methodology, not validated performance findings; its claimed model rankings and success rates are not used as evidence.
qs: [LOW-RELIABILITY — DERIVATIVE OF HARVEY LAB, DO NOT CITE FOR ITS RESULTS]

kp.k: Legal capability allegedly shifted toward end-to-end work
kp.d: The author asserts that legal-agent capability changed in late 2025 after two years of flat long-horizon completion, attributing the change to frontier reasoning models, longer contexts, improved tool use and evaluation infrastructure. This is the article's historical capability claim, framed through an analogy with coding agents rather than independently established evidence.
qs: Long-horizon legal completion was flat for two years. Then in late 2025, frontier reasoning models, longer contexts, better tool use, and proper evaluation infrastructure converged. Capability turned.

kp.k: Short tasks inadequately measure delegated legal work
kp.d: The article argues that short-horizon evaluations such as LegalBench, CUAD and LEXam remain useful but do not establish whether an agent can complete a legal assignment. It treats matter reading, issue selection, exclusion of irrelevant information, drafting and factual accuracy as an integrated workflow that should be evaluated together.
qs: They are useful, but they tell you almost nothing about whether an agent can actually run a piece of work.

What happens between that email and the memo is the entire job - reading the matter, finding the issues that matter, ignoring the ones that don't, drafting reviewable work product, and getting every fact right.

kp.d: HAQQ describes a benchmark containing 1,372 tasks across 24 practice areas and approximately 78,000 atomic criteria. Tasks purportedly use partner-style instructions averaging approximately 50 words, matter folders containing relevant and peripheral material, and reviewable outputs such as memos, redlines or pleadings. Expert rubrics encode partner review for benchmarking; that design does not itself establish safe reliance on outputs in practice.
qs: The HAQQ Legal Agent Study: 1,372 long-horizon legal tasks, 24 practice areas, ~78,000 atomic pass/fail rubric criteria.
Instructions: ~50 words on average. Affirmative ask, no checklist.

Each row is a 1:1 encoding of how a real matter moves through a firm: partner request becomes instruction, client matter becomes environment, work product becomes output, partner review becomes expert rubric.

kp.k: All-pass grading prioritizes complete issue coverage
kp.d: The proposed scoring rule fails a task if any rubric criterion fails. The author justifies this strict threshold by arguing that omitted risks can determine a transaction's viability or valuation, making partial issue detection an inadequate measure of usefulness. This is a normative benchmark-design rationale, not a demonstrated general rule about all legal work.
qs: A task is marked complete only if every rubric criterion passes.

A deal-team report that catches 8 of 10 risks is not 80% useful. The two missed could be the change-of-control trigger that blows up the deal, or the going-concern qualification that reprices the offer.

kp.k: Practitioner rubrics connect assessment with model training
kp.d: The article says practitioners decomposed deliverables into atomic, binary checks reflecting what partners or clients scrutinize. It argues these checks improve reproducibility, identify specific failures and provide fine-tuning reward signals, explicitly connecting benchmark design with subsequent agent development.
qs: For each task we sat down with practitioners in the relevant area and broke down what a partner or client would actually scrutinise in the deliverable.

Atomic criteria do three things at once: they make grading reproducible across runs, they make agent failures debuggable (you see exactly which check broke and why), and they double as reward signals for fine-tuning.

kp.k: Jurisdictional coverage is presented as a differentiation strategy
kp.d: HAQQ argues that US-common-law dominance in existing benchmarks does not match its customers' practices. It describes six explicitly civil-law and MENA families among its 24 areas: Arabic civil-law drafting, Sharia compliance, GCC corporate, construction litigation, family/personal status and MENA labour. It claims tasks were derived from anonymized, sanitized customer matters and acknowledges that coverage is not exhaustive.
qs: Existing legal benchmarks are dominated by US common-law tasks.
We started from real matters - anonymized, sanitized - handled by practicing lawyers across our customer base.
The 24 areas are not exhaustive.
HAQQ's contribution is the multilingual, civil-law, MENA-first axis that has been missing.

kp.k: Illustrative transaction tests synthesis rather than clause recognition
kp.d: A fictional USD 458 million all-equity acquisition of Crestview Software Solutions illustrates the proposed workflow: eight material contracts plus adjacent files feed a deal-team memo with risk mapping, severity ratings and mitigations. The article describes 57 criteria covering nine planted legal issues, requiring cross-document reasoning, financial quantification and recommended action rather than isolated keyword detection.
qs: The rubric for that single task contains 57 criteria - covering nine planted legal issues, the underlying facts behind each, the severity rating, the financial exposure, and the recommended action.
They require the agent to connect facts across documents, infer triggers from definitions, quantify financial exposure in dollars, and recommend the right next legal action.

kp.k: Vendor selection should distinguish delegation from assistance
kp.d: The author recommends that law-firm buyers demand matter-level completion measures and detailed rubric performance rather than single-document demonstrations. The relevant deployment distinction is between tasks claimed to be delegable end-to-end, tasks requiring a lawyer in the loop, and tasks unsuitable for delegation; the article does not establish that benchmark completion removes the need for human verification.
qs: which kinds of work can I delegate end-to-end, which need a lawyer in the loop, and which I shouldn't touch?
Ask them what their all-pass rate is on a 50-criterion rubric for that matter. Ask them which practice areas they cover end-to-end versus only assist.

kp.k: Reported protocol and disclosure remain qualified
kp.d: The article describes testing six systems with three attempts per task and reporting best-of-three all-pass rates, rather than single-attempt completion. It also places release of task-family documentation and rubric format under an evaluation licence in the future, alongside a normalized methodology and baseline leaderboard. These are stated protocol and disclosure conditions, not independent validation of the article's results.
qs: Each task was attempted three times; we report best-of-three all-pass rate.
v1 task families and rubric format are documented and will be released to customers and research partners under an evaluation licence.
We will publish a normalized scoring methodology and a baseline leaderboard once we have results from all major frontier models.

kp.k: Expansion into in-house and multilingual workflows is planned
kp.d: HAQQ presents additional jurisdictional and buyer-side workflow coverage as future development, not current demonstrated capability. Its stated v2 plans include MENA arbitration, construction disputes, in-house counsel workflows and broader Arabic and French civil-law drafting, with selected law firms contributing extensions.
qs: v2 will add MENA arbitration, construction disputes, in-house counsel workflows, and broader Arabic and French civil-law drafting.
We are co-developing extensions with selected law firms - if you want to contribute task families from your practice, get in touch.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Boghossian claims legal AI is moving toward end-to-end completion of delegated legal work, with specialised agents better suited than generic models to long-horizon and civil-law tasks.
pts.d: Writing for HAQQ, Stephane Boghossian claims that improvements in reasoning, context length, tool use and evaluation infrastructure produced an inflection in legal-agent capability. He argues that short-horizon tests provide little information about whether an agent can complete a matter-based assignment, and that domain-trained agents reduce failures on longer workflows, especially civil-law drafting. He presents long-horizon benchmarking as a way to distinguish work suitable for end-to-end delegation from work requiring lawyer involvement. These are attributed source claims, not established findings. The supplied document explicitly labels this source low-reliability and derivative of Harvey Lab and instructs that its results not be cited; numerical performance results are therefore not reproduced.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article offers HAQQ's own benchmark, practitioner-designed rubrics and a worked transaction example as support.
pts.d: Boghossian describes matter-based tasks requiring agents to select relevant documents and produce reviewable deliverables. The stated evidence basis is an internal vendor evaluation using expert-written, atomic pass/fail criteria, with every criterion required for task completion and best-of-three attempts reported. A change-of-control example illustrates cross-document reasoning, financial exposure calculations and recommended legal actions. Practitioners are said to have contributed matters and rubrics. This is benchmarking of model outputs, rather than evidence of actual changes in law-firm employment, prices or deployed productivity. The article uses rubric checking to represent partner review; that should not be conflated with demonstrated human verification in live practice. Its performance results are not cited because of the supplied source restriction.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claimed capability shift begins in late 2025; the May 2026 article conditions delegation on task-specific, practice-specific completion rather than generic model fluency.
pts.d: The article dates the claimed inflection to late 2025 after two years of flat long-horizon completion. Its current-capability claims concern the study's v1 environment and all-pass, best-of-three protocol, not guaranteed success on a single real-world attempt. It explicitly distinguishes end-to-end coverage from assistance and acknowledges that practice-area coverage is not exhaustive. Wider workflow and jurisdictional coverage, release of evaluation materials and publication of a normalised methodology and leaderboard are future plans without firm delivery dates.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law-firm partners and associates, legal-AI buyers and vendors, and practitioners serving civil-law and MENA matters.
pts.d: Partners are presented as deciding which assignments to delegate to agents and which require a lawyer in the loop. Associate-type work—reviewing matter files, identifying issues and drafting deliverables—is the target of the proposed automation, although the article makes no explicit headcount or staffing prediction. Legal-AI buyers are urged to demand matter-level completion evidence rather than single-document demonstrations. Vendors are expected to substantiate practice-specific coverage. Civil-law and MENA practitioners are positioned as beneficiaries of jurisdiction-specific systems, while in-house workflows are an intended future extension. Client exposure to missed legal risks motivates strict grading, but the article does not quantify client savings or access-to-justice effects.
